name: Musgu
confidence_why: Tourneux 1978, the only modern first-hand description, gives every Mulwi syllable one of four tonemes on two registers with lexical minimal pairs and never mentions stress, and Tourneux 1991 calls the Cameroon Munjuk of Pouss a tone language too, so the sole contrary statement, a tendency to stress the final syllable of isolated nouns and adjectives in Krause's 1880s travel notes edited by Müller 1886, is an untrained pre-phonemic report that the modern grammar outweighs.

catalog_quote: Tourneux 1978 §3.1: "Chaque syllabe, en mulwi, est affectée d'un ton. L'analyse permet de dégager deux registres tonals (Haut) et (Bas) par rapport auxquels se situent quatre tonèmes (ou tons): Haut, Bas, Descendant, Montant. Il n'y aurait pas d'inconvénient à analyser les deux tonèmes modulés en une succession de deux mores: Haut + Bas = Descendant, Bas + Haut = Montant. Si un locuteur vloum récite la numération de 1 à 10, dans l'absolu, il affectera le chiffre "trois" hu d'un ton supra-haut. Ce ton supra-haut se réduira à un ton haut dans le flux normal du discours." || Müller 1886 p. [359], 'Betonung der Wörter': "In dem einzeln gesprochenen Worte herrscht beim Substantivum und Adjectivum das Bestreben vor, die letzte Silbe zu betonen, im Zusammenhang der Rede aber scheint der Accent keiner bestimmten Silbe anzugehören. Durch das Betonen der letzten Silbe wird ein schnelles Hinweggleiten der Stimme über die Anfangssilben bedingt, und daher sind hier lange Vocale sowie Doppelconsonanten, welche beide ein Verweilen der Stimme bedingen, selten."

new_statements.translation: Word stress. In the word spoken in isolation, nouns and adjectives show a prevailing tendency to stress the last syllable; in connected speech, however, the accent seems to belong to no particular syllable. Stressing the last syllable causes the voice to glide quickly over the initial syllables, and therefore long vowels and double consonants, both of which require the voice to linger, are rare there. This hastiness of the language makes it extremely hard to catch the vowels of the first syllables [...]

new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation forms, nouns and adjectives tend to carry prominence on the final syllable, with reduced/hurried pretonic syllables; in connected speech no fixed stress position is discernible. (Pre-tonal 1886 description based on Krause's notes from displaced speakers; modern descriptions — Tourneux 1978, 1991 — analyse Musgu/Munjuk as a tone language with H, L, rising and falling tonemes and make no statement about stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: Statement restricted to nouns and adjectives in isolation; in connected speech 'the accent seems to belong to no particular syllable'; in the copular/verbalised paradigm Müller notes (p. ~378) that 'der Ton' may also rest on the subject verbal pronoun. Krause marks accent ad hoc with an acute in some transcriptions (e.g. tsémana, proper names).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation (isolation) forms of nouns/adjectives only; explicitly not phrase-level. Source predates tonal analysis; what Krause heard as final 'Betonung' may reflect tone/final prominence in a language now described as tonal (Tourneux 1978 ch. 3: 'Chaque syllabe, en mulwi, est affectée d'un ton'; Tourneux 1991: 'Le munjuk est une langue à tons').
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress statement (Müller 1886) rests on G. A. Krause's notes taken in Tripoli from freed Musgu ('Musuk') slaves, chiefly Ali Mut of Ngilemong village near Kadé on the Logone (Cameroon-side Musgu proper, musg1254). The modern descriptions examined cover other varieties of the same language: Tourneux 1978 = Mulwi/Vulum of Mogroum (Chad; Glottolog dialect 'Vulum'), Tourneux 1991 = Munjuk 'des rizières', Pouss dialect (Cameroon; 'Mpus'). All fall under musg1254.

tone_statements.citation: Tourneux, Henri (1976). Phonologie du muwli de Mogroum (Tchad). Univ. de la Sorbonne Nouvelle (Paris 3).
tone_statements.quote: Chaque syllabe, en mulwi, est affectée d'un ton. L'analyse permet de dégager deux registres tonals (Haut) et (Bas) par rapport auxquels se situent quatre tonèmes (ou tons) : / ´ / Haut, / ` / Bas, / ˆ / Descendant, / ˇ / Montant. Il n'y aurait pas d'inconvénient à analyser les deux tonèmes modulés en une succession de deux mores: Haut + Bas = Descendant, Bas + Haut = Montant. [...] 3.2 La langue utilise les tons à des fins distinctives, généralement, et les exemples suivants en prouveront la pertinence phonologique. [section 3.27:] Le rendement distinctif des oppositions tonales n'est pas très important dans le lexique. Il est par contre très fort en grammaire, puisque l'on peut dire, en simplifiant, que l'opposition Haut / Bas est la marque de l'opposition "inaccompli" / "accompli".

readall_conflicts: No direct conflict. Müller/Krause 1886 (already in existing_statements) reports a tendency to stress the final syllable of isolated nouns and adjectives with no fixed accent in connected speech, for the Cameroon Musuk; Tourneux 1978 describes the Chad Mulwi/Vulum of Mogroum purely in terms of four tonemes on two registers and says nothing about stress or accent. The two sources talk past each other (an 1880s 'Betonung' report from a non-linguist's notes versus a 1978 tonological analysis of a different dialect), so the catalog's existing final-stress reading rests on Müller 1886 alone and is not supported or refuted by the modern description.

sources.quote: (2) Bases derived from vowel-less roots to form adverbials and verbonominals have no inherent distinctive tone or tone pattern, but are simply accompanied by pitch realisations which reflect the underlying consonant structure (cf 1 above). Grammatical morphemes such as the suffix -i which forms verbonominal stems from verbonominal bases, do have distinctive tone. [...] All this explains why today's Vulum exhibits so many tonal minimally contrastive pairs the existence of which one normally takes as a clear indication for the presence of distinctive tones, although in the lexicon of this language, at least in its verbal section, no tones need to be indicated if one chose to give underlying representations of roots or bases therein.

tone.quote: 2.7. Eastern Central Chadic is represented by Musgu. ... There are again three types of consonants to be distinguished : depressors (voiced obstruents), non-depressors (voiceless obstruents), and neutral consonants (sonorants). Cf. the following verbal nouns which clearly show the effect of the word-initial consonant on tone : depressor L zìrí "aligner" L vìnì "prendre" non-depressor H sírí "écraser" H fíní "rester" neutral L yìmì "attraper" H yímí "être beau" The last pair of examples shows how tonal contrast development starts off from the neutral class by phonologizing and lexicalizing prosodic alternations of segmental homophones.
